slides.title: A waveform can contain several rhythms
slides.lead: Frequency analysis asks how strongly each periodic component is present.
slides.notes: Change amplitude and DC separately. Ask which change should move a spectral peak and which should only change its height or DC bin.

slides.title: Amplitude, frequency, phase and offset
points: A controls excursion; f controls cycles per second
φ shifts the waveform in time; c shifts the baseline
A sum of sinusoids is still one time-domain signal
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Compute a spectrum from the samples
slides.lead: This demonstration recomputes a discrete Fourier transform from the generated array.
points: The lab uses NumPy’s efficient real FFT for the same transform
Magnitude is unnormalised, matching np.abs(rfft(...))
Inspect the two peaks; change frequency away from a bin center
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Why remove the mean?
slides.lead: The mean occupies the zero-frequency bin.
points: For acceleration magnitude, gravity creates a large baseline
Subtracting the mean removes DC without removing all low-frequency motion
This operation is different from per-window variance normalisation
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Real input needs only half the spectrum
slides.lead: N=100 real samples produce N//2+1 = 51 bins.
points: The negative-frequency half is redundant for real-valued input
abs converts complex coefficients into nonnegative magnitudes
The plotted spectrum is not a probability distribution
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Build the frequency axis
points: d is the sample spacing in seconds, not the sampling frequency
Bin k corresponds to k·fs/N
For odd N, the last bin lies below fs/2
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Resolution costs observation time
points: A 2 s window gives 0.5 Hz spacing; 4 s gives 0.25 Hz
More samples at the same rate mean a longer wait
Finer bin spacing alone does not guarantee separation of noisy nearby tones
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: The strongest non-DC bin
slides.lead: Exclude bin zero, then restore the index offset.
points: mag[1:] starts at bin 1, but argmax returns a local index
Add 1 before indexing the full frequency array
For nearly flat noise, a largest bin exists without meaningful periodic motion
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Aliasing: different curves, identical samples
slides.lead: A 40 Hz signal sampled at 50 Hz can appear at 10 Hz.
points: Sample faster or filter before sampling
A digital FFT cannot recover information already lost in acquisition
The Nyquist boundary is not a comfortable operating margin
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: What happens between FFT bins?
slides.lead: A finite observation window can spread a tone across bins.
points: The lab uses a rectangular window: no taper is applied
Try 5.75 Hz over 2 s: it is between 5.5 and 6.0 Hz
A Hann window is an optional extension, with amplitude/bandwidth trade-offs
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Magnitude can double the shake frequency
slides.lead: Both positive and negative sideways excursions increase √(ax²+g²).
points: For a mostly sideways shake with stable gravity, |a| rises twice per cycle
The bundled shake spectrum peaks near 11.5 Hz
Use ax for the fundamental hand-motion frequency; doubling is not universal
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: The model sees time series, not this FFT
points: Order: ax, ay, az, gx, gy, gz
Fixed scaling: acceleration ÷ 9.80665; gyro ÷ 4
SDK normalise clips to ±4; the lab heatmap displays −2…2
The heatmap is a view of model input, not an image passed to a vision CNN
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

slides.title: Run Lab 9.2
slides.lead: This lab analyses files even when --replay is omitted.
points: Default: first 100 samples of each bundled gesture
A custom take can replace the default files
Compare the |a| spectrum and the six-channel input heatmap
slides.notes: Ask students to explain why a synthetic idle file still has a nonzero largest frequency bin. Avoid describing this script as live acquisition.

slides.title: Frequency self-check
slides.lead: At 50 Hz, what does a 3 s window provide?
slides.notes: Ask students to predict the result before revealing or running it. Connect the observation to the lab source linked on this slide.

quiz.explanation: N=50×3=150; bins=N//2+1=76; spacing=fs/N=1/3 Hz. Nyquist remains 25 Hz.
